title: No Impact Required: ESA Funds $891,000 Ion-Beam Asteroid Deflection Study That Could Let Scientists Choose Where a Space Rock Lands
excerpt: ESA ion-beam asteroid deflection gets its first formal study: the European Space Agency has opened an $891,000 tender for Anubis, a spacecraft concept that nudges asteroids off course without touching them and could steer where a threat lands, not just whether it misses Earth. Bids close December
content:
A spacecraft that never touches an asteroid could still move it. That is the premise behind ion-beam shepherding (IBS), and it is now the subject of a formal European Space Agency procurement tender. ESA has posted a €800,000 (approximately $891,000) contract notice for a Phase A feasibility study of a mission concept called Anubis, inviting aerospace firms to design a spacecraft that would deflect a threatening asteroid using nothing but a focused beam of charged particles. The bid deadline is December 2, 2026, at 13:00 CET.

Ion-beam shepherding is not new in concept — the idea was first formalized in a foundational 2011 asteroid deflection paper by researchers Claudio Bombardelli and Jesús Peláez at the Technical University of Madrid — but no mission has yet tested it in space. Anubis would be the first to do so, and its proponents argue it fills a gap that the celebrated NASA DART mission left open.

How Ion-Beam Shepherding Actually Works

An Anubis-class spacecraft would carry a xenon ion thruster pointed at an asteroid and a secondary thruster pointed in the opposite direction. The forward thruster fires a continuous stream of ions directly at the asteroid's surface. When those ions strike and partially embed, they transfer momentum to the rock — a modern application of the same Tsiolkovsky principle that governs every rocket ever flown. The secondary thruster fires to cancel out the recoil that would otherwise push the spacecraft backward into the asteroid. The net effect: the asteroid drifts. Slowly, over months or years, by a calculable fraction of a millimeter per second per day, the cumulative deflection becomes enough to shift a planetary close approach by tens of thousands of kilometers.

The technology lineage is well established. NASA's Dawn spacecraft demonstrated that ion drives could operate continuously for years at high efficiency in deep space; Japan's Hayabusa asteroid probe showed that ion propulsion could manage the delicate proximity operations required near a small, low-gravity body. IBS applies both lessons simultaneously, adding a second thruster to maintain the standoff geometry required for sustained force delivery.

The key advantage over kinetic impact is composition independence. DART worked by colliding a spacecraft with Dimorphos at roughly 6.1 kilometers per second. The resulting momentum transfer depended critically on ejecta amplification — essentially, how much debris the impact blasted back off the surface, which multiplied the deflection force. That multiplier, known as the beta factor, varies enormously depending on whether the target is solid rock, loosely consolidated rubble, or something in between. A rubble-pile asteroid absorbs a kinetic impact differently than a monolith, potentially yielding a beta close to 1 (no amplification) rather than the roughly 3.6 value DART achieved. Ion beams sidestep this entirely: the momentum transfer does not depend on the asteroid's internal structure or surface composition.

A Third Tool in the Planetary Defense Kit

The case for IBS rests partly on what DART demonstrated and partly on what it could not. When NASA's impactor struck Dimorphos on September 26, 2022, it shortened the moonlet's orbital period by approximately 33 minutes — NASA's threshold for mission success was just 73 seconds, so the actual result exceeded that threshold by more than 27 times. The mission validated kinetic impact as a viable deflection strategy.

What it could not do was aim. A kinetic impactor deflects a target along the vector defined by the impact geometry; the deflected object ends up wherever the orbital mechanics put it. For the DART demonstration, this was not a concern — Dimorphos poses no Earth-impact threat and the goal was merely to change its period by a measurable amount. But for a real planetary defense scenario, mission designers might want to steer a threat away from a specific populated corridor rather than just off Earth entirely. ESA's Hera follow-on mission, currently en route to the Didymos system with a December 2026 arrival, will characterize the full aftermath of the DART impact and refine estimates of how precisely a kinetic impactor can be aimed.

Ion-beam shepherding, by contrast, is inherently steerable. A spacecraft can be repositioned relative to the asteroid, changing the thrust vector — and thus the deflection direction — in real time. A 2026 SMPAG mission scenarios study published in Acta Astronautica (Vol. 242) documented mission architectures in which IBS could be used not merely to deflect an impactor but to redirect it toward a low-population oceanic impact zone rather than a densely settled landmass. This partial-deflection capability — steering where the rock goes rather than simply whether it hits — is the scenario where IBS has no kinetic-impact equivalent.

Context: ESA's Expanding Planetary Defense Investment

Anubis sits within a broader ESA planetary defense push funded through ESA's CM25 planetary defense proposal, adopted at the 2025 Ministerial Council. The Space Safety Programme, of which planetary defense is a core pillar, received increased allocation at CM25, enabling both mission studies like Anubis and operational investments in telescope networks and early-warning infrastructure.

The most visible recent commitment was ESA's award to OHB Italia the RAMSES contract, announced in February 2026 for a mission to rendezvous with asteroid Apophis during its historic 2029 flyby — when the 340-meter space rock will pass within approximately 32,000 kilometers of Earth's surface, well inside the orbital distance of geostationary satellites. RAMSES will study Apophis at close range before, during, and after the flyby, measuring how Earth's tidal forces and gravitational gradient reshape the asteroid's rotation, surface structure, and orbital trajectory. The data is scientifically unprecedented but also directly applicable to deflection planning: knowing how Apophis responds to Earth's gravity during a close pass informs models of how it would respond to an artificial force applied by a spacecraft like Anubis.

The commercial sector is also moving in. Blue Origin announced NEO Hunter in March 2026, a planetary defense concept built on its Blue Ring orbital platform in partnership with NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory and Caltech. NEO Hunter combines ion-beam propulsion with a kinetic disruption backup — a hybrid architecture that reflects similar thinking to Anubis but from a commercial contractor perspective. ESA's parallel investment through the Anubis tender suggests that government space agencies regard IBS as a credible enough concept to advance through formal procurement channels, not merely academic study.

What Anubis Must Answer

A Phase A study is a feasibility investigation, not a funded mission. The Anubis contract will pay up to €800,000 for a team to develop a credible spacecraft concept: identifying the right target asteroid for a demonstration mission, defining the thruster specifications and standoff geometry, characterizing the operational constraints of sustained ion-beam contact over months-long proximity operations, and estimating the minimum lead time and deflection magnitude achievable with realistic technology development timelines.

Several technical questions remain open. Ion engines designed for deep-space cruise operate in a different regime than an engine designed to fire continuously at a fixed target while a second thruster holds station. The mass budget — how much propellant a spacecraft must carry to deliver a meaningful deflection impulse over a multi-month mission — drives the entire launch architecture and determines which existing or planned rockets could deliver the system to a threat scenario's required intercept point. Researchers at JAXA and a team at CNES have both published preliminary models suggesting that a 1,000 kg spacecraft with a 200 mN thruster could deflect a 150-meter rubble-pile asteroid by a planetary-radius distance given roughly 10 years of warning time, but those estimates carry significant uncertainty bands depending on asteroid bulk density assumptions.

The winning bidder will address all of this and define the path from feasibility study to Phase B/C detailed design. ESA has not committed to any subsequent mission phases; the Anubis tender is a study contract only. What it represents is a formal institutional bet that contactless deflection is worth understanding at the level of hardware, not just equations.

The Anubis Phase A study tender is listed on ESA's EMITS procurement portal with bid deadline December 2, 2026, 13:00 CET.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is ion-beam shepherding?

Ion-beam shepherding (IBS) is an asteroid deflection technique that uses a focused stream of charged xenon ions fired from a spacecraft to push an asteroid off course. Unlike a kinetic impactor, the spacecraft never touches the asteroid — it maintains a fixed standoff distance while the ion beam continuously transfers momentum to the target. A secondary thruster on the opposite side of the spacecraft fires simultaneously to cancel out the recoil, keeping the spacecraft in position.

How is ESA's Anubis mission different from NASA's DART mission?

DART was a kinetic impactor — it physically collided with the asteroid Dimorphos. The deflection force DART delivered depended partly on how much debris the impact kicked up from the surface, which varies with an asteroid's composition and structure. Anubis uses an ion beam, which transfers momentum regardless of whether the asteroid is solid rock or a loosely bound rubble pile. Anubis also offers steering capability: by repositioning the spacecraft relative to the asteroid, mission controllers can adjust the direction of the deflection force, potentially steering a threat toward a low-population oceanic zone rather than simply moving it off Earth entirely.

Why is a Phase A study significant?

A Phase A study is ESA's first formal procurement and feasibility phase for a new mission concept. It moves a technology from academic papers into the domain of spacecraft engineering, requiring a team to design a credible hardware concept, identify a target asteroid, define operational constraints, and produce a cost and schedule framework. For ion-beam shepherding, which has never been tested in space, completing a Phase A study would be the most concrete step toward an eventual demonstration mission.

What is the bid deadline for the Anubis contract?

The contract notice posted on ESA's EMITS procurement portal lists a bid deadline of December 2, 2026, at 13:00 CET. The contract value is €800,000, approximately $891,000 at the exchange rate applicable at time of writing.

What other asteroid missions are ESA currently working on?

ESA is developing the RAMSES mission, which will rendezvous with the near-Earth asteroid Apophis during its record-close 2029 flyby of Earth. RAMSES received a contract award to OHB Italia in February 2026 and will study how Apophis responds to Earth's gravitational and tidal forces during the flyby. ESA's Hera spacecraft is also already en route to the Didymos system to study the aftermath of NASA's DART impact on the moonlet Dimorphos, with arrival expected in December 2026.
